set.st: Frank G. Stocking (Morgan Hill, Cal., 1914), whose family knew Wabasis, wrote that the chief's oldest daughter told his grandmother the money (silver, in a copper kettle covered with moss) was taken by canoe up the creek and buried. He hunted it and left a pick and shovel there about 1879. The 1922 nephew account says gold in a tin pail inside an iron kettle. In January 1889 a state-news wire said two Rockford men thought they knew where the fortune lay and were digging for it; no outcome was reported. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself. A 1922 family account adds that the chief later moved the kettle of silver by canoe 'up the creek'; nobody knew where. Spot from Stocking's 1914 directions: 1/2 to 3/4 mile up Wabasis Creek from the Little Wabasis outlet, about 10 rods off the creek. Creek course from the 1972 USGS topo, so it may have shifted since the 1870s. About 1918 a party from New York came to Belding claiming to know the spot, then suddenly packed up and left; many locals believed they got it (unconfirmed). The 1880 telling (earliest print found): the chief received about $10,000 at Grand Rapids for tribal lands, put it in a strong box and sank it in Wahnoketo (Wabasis) Lake; he was killed for it and his bones later found on the shore; 'no trace of the treasure'. The paper's sequel of a man digging up an oak coffer of gold is a comic tall tale, not a find. Jud W. King's 1922 defence of the chief gives the nephew's account in full: about 1890 the old Methodist preacher near Kiddville told King the treaty gold filled an eight-quart tin pail to within 2½ inches of the top, set inside a covered iron kettle; after the eloping daughter took some, Wabasis dug it up to show the tribe, then he and his crippled son reburied it in a new place; Wabasis was stabbed pursuing the couple and the son died soon after without telling. A 1921 Lakeview Enterprise piece has him burying it 'somewhere along the shores of the lake he loved' (per his rival Neoggamah), with the shores 'dug up in various places, yet no trace'. The Belding Banner (4 Oct 1916) says Barney Race and Ed Whitford probed the shore of Little Wabasis Lake for the kettle; the 1922 Stocking letter names the Olsgaard farm north of Belding as the family place. The 11 March 1914 Banner (continued on p. 9) tells of a third hunt: after seances and an Ionia gunsmith's divining rod failed, a Belding man dreamed the spot, the north bank of Little Wabasis Lake, a small flat with softwood trees and an abrupt rise behind, a lone six-inch tree with the pot four feet down at its base. He and a local doctor rowed over and probed more than a thousand spots over a week and found nothing; they believed the iron box had rusted away and the pot still lay in that hillside.

pinev: Placed from the source text: Frank G. Stocking letter 1914: "south side of the creek about 1/2 or 3/4 of a mile above the lake and about 10 rods back from the creek"; camp on E side of Little Wabasis Lake (GNIS 43.1539,-85.3594). Pin = creek midway between the lakes

1876 Kent atlas, Oakfield T9N R9W: the inlet creek runs S from Oakfield Centre past Little Wabasis (sec 22) and enters the lake's NE lobe in NW sec 27, matching the pin's reach (the pin is in the S of sec 22, BLM PLSS). Stocking's 'south side of the creek' 1/2-3/4 mi above the lake falls on the Norton and Cooper land (Jas. Norton 160 in NW sec 27; Jno. Norton 80 and H. Cooper 20 in S sec 22 E of the creek); no Stocking tract.
1894 and 1907 Kent plats: no Stocking land at the creek; a Parmus Stocking lived in Oakfield Twp in 1900 (census).
1880 census: Parmus T. Stocking in Grattan Twp (Oakfield by 1900); Frank Stocking, b. 1860 at Otisco/Belding, is likely the F. G. Stocking of the 1914 letter.
Third candidate from the 1914 dream dig: north bank of Little Wabasis Lake (small flat, abrupt rise); dream-guided, so no pin of its own.
